extracted.intended_audience: mathematics faculty and graduate students (early-career academics) seeking practical professional advice on conferences, textbook writing, curriculum, service, and letters
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for mathematicians on attending major meetings, writing textbooks, redesigning curricula, serving the department, and composing professional letters of recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding to attend the January Joint Mathematics Meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: The AMS and MAA jointly sponsor a large January meeting lasting about four days (with preliminary activities); it is very well attended and draws a broad cross-section of the profession, invited lectures, special sessions, panels, a huge exhibit area, networking, social events, and excursions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample panels and special sessions (they can be stimulating and informative); visit the exhibit area (publishers, government agencies, summer programs, software makers) — useful for meeting publishers if you plan to publish; registration (≈$200) is required for many events and name tag access; students/retirees get reduced fee; seek department support or AMS grants to help cover expenses; consider organizing a group or bringing family to make it more enjoyable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation for writing a textbook
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbook writing is a different, time-consuming enterprise and 'is not something to be entered lightly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer non-pecuniary motives: desire to change how a subject is taught, having something important to say, or wanting to have an impact on the profession. Such motives are likelier to sustain you through the long project than money alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose textbook level with realistic expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower-division (freshman/sophomore) textbooks are a highly competitive market and publishers are selective; upper-division and graduate texts offer more author control and generally fewer drafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower-division books usually require more rigorous publishing processes (many reviewers/developmental editors) and may take longer; an upper-division text can sometimes be produced in as little as two years and involves fewer drafts; graduate texts are 'even more gentle' and focus more on mathematics content and exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing realities and market considerations for textbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers are profit-driven; sales volumes dictate publisher interest and what gets marketed. Successful lower-division texts can sell ~50,000 copies/year; successful upper-division texts ~5,000 copies/year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers need to cover 'plant costs' (editors, typesetting, design, printing, warehousing) before profit — books must meet sales thresholds. There are far fewer publishers willing to take on monographs or upper-division texts today than in the past; developmental (remedial) math is where the real market money is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbook production practicalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing a textbook involves many practical issues beyond content: wrestling with reviewers and developmental editors, design choices (e.g., use of color), copyright clearances for figures, and legalities for borrowed material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult experienced colleagues and existing resources; be prepared for extensive editorial involvement to make the manuscript marketable; expect negotiations over design and permissions; meet publishers at conferences to discuss these matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess departmental and community support before redesigning curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: Curriculum redesign is a protracted undertaking that requires gauging departmental interest and support before investing large amounts of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form a team, take the temperature of the entire department (faculty meeting), obtain approval or buy-in from the Chair and Executive Committee, and consider running major proposals by the Dean. Avoid spending years on proposals if the department is content with the status quo — this can cause damaging rifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue external funding for curriculum reform
rubrics_metrics.description: There is government and private foundation money available to support curriculum revitalization efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider writing grants to secure substantial support (the text notes examples of multi-million dollar grants). Understand the potential institutional effects (infrastructure changes, resentments) and have a clear sense of what you are getting into before pursuing large grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to be a departmental citizen
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee work and administrative duties are part of academic life and should be performed professionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do your homework and contribute constructively on committees; initiating programs or curricular projects is appropriate but clear such activities with the Chair (and possibly the Executive Committee) first; departmental service counts toward tenure/promotion but typically less than research and publications; balance service with your primary mission to do and teach mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to decline writing a professional letter
rubrics_metrics.description: There are circumstances when you cannot or should not write a letter: personal conflicts, conflicts of interest, unfamiliarity with the candidate's area, not knowing the candidate well, or having a poor opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quickly and plainly inform the person (Dean or Chair) who requested the letter that you cannot write; if asked in person, give an honest answer right away. Do not accept a request you cannot fulfill; give a reason if feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and process for letters of recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: If you agree to write a letter, do so in a timely fashion; do not delay or accept and then not deliver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'shilly-shallying' for months; some faculty use interactive web forms for letter requests (have students fill in background info, courses taken, grades, extracurriculars, distinctions) to streamline the process and reduce legwork — this can provide a useful draft and tracking mechanism for requested letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters of recommendation — open with purpose and thesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by stating plainly the purpose of the letter and your overall recommendation (thesis) in the first few sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: explicitly state e.g. 'The purpose of this letter is to support the tenure and promotion of X... I indeed think that tenure and promotion are appropriate' or conversely state a negative thesis. The opening must make clear what question you are addressing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters of recommendation — support thesis with specific evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The body of the letter should support the opening thesis with detailed, specific remarks about the candidate's work, contributions, qualities, and objective qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss particular papers and explain why results are important, how they improve on earlier work, who else has worked on the problem, and the significance; provide objective information (publications, journals, teaching record); be precise and only speak to topics of direct knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters of recommendation — include a concluding paragraph restating the case
rubrics_metrics.description: End with a concluding paragraph that sums up the case, re-states the thesis, and emphasizes your recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the conclusion explicit (examples: strong recommendation for promotion and tenure, or clear statement recommending against). Do not omit the summation — 'You must write it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters of recommendation — make binary comparisons to peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong letters should compare the candidate to other people of similar age and career level, preferably naming recognizable peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give comparisons that convey rank or placement (e.g., 'the five best people under the age of 35 in this area are A, B, C, D, E' or 'Candidate X fits between Y and Z'); such comparisons help nonspecialist evaluators and carry persuasive force when names are recognizable in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters of recommendation — avoid vague praise ('damning with faint praise')
rubrics_metrics.description: Vague, noncommittal praise is unhelpful and can be construed as negative or evasive, leaving evaluators to guess your meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If uncomfortable about making a candid assessment, consider declining to write rather than writing a vague letter. If you do write, be explicit and detailed so evaluators are not left to interpret faint praise; if soliciting institution may allow candidate access to letters, you are offered the option of declining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters of recommendation — write for nonspecialist readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Many readers of letters (Deans, committee members) will be nonspecialists, so provide brief background, motivation, and context for the candidate's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain significance in accessible terms, drop some recognizable names for context, and note publication venues (e.g., Annals) to signal quality; keep explanations brief but informative so non-experts can appreciate the candidate's accomplishments.
